claims.page_title: ADHD Concerns in Children: First Steps With a GP
claims.claim_text: Can a GP diagnose ADHD? Assessment pathways vary. A GP can start the process, check for overlapping issues and refer to clinicians who assess and manage ADHD.

primary_source.title: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (GP Factsheet)

supporting_source.title: Australian evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

claims.evidence_summary: The 2022 Australian ADHD Guideline supports GPs having a role in identification, and in some circumstances diagnosis and prescribing; however, formal diagnosis of children commonly involves paediatricians/psychiatrists and prescribing of stimulants is subject to state/territory authority rules (e.g. NSW stimulant prescribing regulations). The article's cautious wording ('assessment pathways vary', 'a GP can start the process ... and refer') is accurate and does not overstate GP scope.
claims.limitations: GP diagnostic/prescribing scope varies by state/territory and individual training; the article intentionally avoids specifics, which is appropriate.
claims.reviewer_notes: Wording is deliberately conservative and defensible. If desired, the guideline now permits suitably trained GPs to diagnose/manage in some cases, but leaving this out avoids AHPRA scope-of-practice risk. Keep as is.

claims.page_title: ADHD Concerns in Children: First Steps With a GP
claims.claim_text: Seek urgent help if your child is at risk of harming themselves or others, has severe aggression that cannot be safely managed, is expressing suicidal thoughts, or there are serious safety concerns at home or school.
claims.recommended_wording: If your child is in immediate danger, is expressing suicidal thoughts, is at risk of harming themselves or others, or has severe aggression that cannot be safely managed, seek urgent help now: call 000 or go to your nearest emergency department. You can also call the Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800 (any time) or Lifeline on 13 11 14. If there are serious safety concerns at home or school, please raise them promptly with your GP or the relevant service.

primary_source.title: Kids Health Info: Suicide and self-harm - helping your child

claims.evidence_summary: The red-flag list identifies clinically appropriate situations for urgent escalation. However for suicidal thoughts or acute risk of harm, best practice is to give an unambiguous emergency pathway (call 000 / go to ED) plus named crisis lines rather than only 'seek urgent help', so a distressed parent knows exactly what to do at 2am.
claims.limitations: Educational; does not replace clinical assessment.
claims.reviewer_notes: Content is correct; strengthen by adding explicit 000/ED instruction and Kids Helpline 1800 55 1800 / Lifeline 13 11 14. Preserves warm first-person practice voice. [Implemented 2026-09-20; applied to site - see corresponding IND entry.]

claims.page_title: Baby and Childhood Eczema: Getting the Basics Right
claims.claim_text: Are steroid creams safe for babies? They can be safe and effective when the right strength is used in the right place for the right time. Ask your GP for a clear plan.
claims.evidence_summary: RCH states topical corticosteroids are effective and safe for children when used correctly (appropriate strength, site and duration). The article's wording mirrors this and correctly directs parents to obtain an individualised plan, directly addressing steroid-phobia myths without overstating safety.
claims.limitations: Safety is conditional on correct strength/site/duration; potent steroids on the face or long unsupervised use carry risk - the article's 'right strength/right place/right time' framing captures this.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate and safely framed. No change needed.

claims.page_title: Baby and Childhood Eczema: Getting the Basics Right
claims.claim_text: Is eczema caused by food allergy? Usually not directly, although food allergy can be relevant for some children. Do not remove major foods without medical advice.
claims.evidence_summary: ASCIA and RCH advise that eczema is a skin barrier condition not usually caused by food allergy, that food allergy is relevant only for some children, and specifically warn against unsupervised elimination of major foods (risk of nutritional harm and of increasing food allergy through avoidance). The article's warning is accurate and safety-protective.
claims.limitations: General; some children do have food-triggered flares warranting assessment.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate and safe. No change needed.

claims.page_title: Baby and Childhood Eczema: Getting the Basics Right
claims.claim_text: Seek prompt care for fever, rapidly worsening redness, swelling, pus, honey-coloured crusting, painful skin, eczema around the eyes, widespread blisters or a child who seems very unwell.
claims.recommended_wording: Seek prompt medical care if there is fever, rapidly worsening redness, swelling, pus, honey-coloured crusting or painful skin, as this can mean the eczema is infected. Seek same-day medical care for widespread blisters or clustered painful blisters, or eczema around the eyes, as these can be a sign of a serious viral skin infection (eczema herpeticum). If your child seems very unwell, is hard to wake, has trouble breathing or a rash that does not fade when pressed, call 000 or go to your nearest emergency department.

primary_source.title: Clinical Practice Guidelines: Eczema (bacterial infection and eczema herpeticum)

supporting_source.title: Atopic eczema in under 12s: diagnosis and management (eczema herpeticum)

claims.evidence_summary: The listed signs correctly capture bacterial infection (weeping, pus, honey-coloured crusting, pain, fever) and eczema herpeticum (widespread/clustered blisters, eczema around the eyes). Guidelines classify eczema herpeticum as requiring same-day treatment and specialist review; the generic 'seek prompt care' understates the urgency for the herpeticum/eye signs. Adding 'same-day' for those signs and a 000/ED pathway for a very unwell child makes the advice clinically safer.
claims.limitations: Educational; clinical assessment still required.
claims.reviewer_notes: Facts are correct; qualification strengthens time-critical wording for eczema herpeticum and periocular involvement. Keeps warm voice. [Implemented 2026-09-20; applied to site - see corresponding IND entry.]

claims.page_title: Childhood Immunisations and Development Checks With a GP
claims.claim_text: Can my child be vaccinated with a mild cold? Often yes, but it depends on symptoms and how unwell the child is. Your GP or nurse can assess on the day.

primary_source.org: Australian Government Department of Health (Australian Immunisation Handbook)
primary_source.title: Preparing for vaccination / Table: Responses to conditions identified through pre-vaccination screening

claims.evidence_summary: The Australian Immunisation Handbook states minor illness (e.g. mild upper respiratory infection with or without low-grade fever) is NOT a contraindication and vaccination can proceed; a moderate or severe acute illness (with or without fever) is a precaution and may warrant deferral. The article's 'often yes, depends on symptoms/how unwell, GP or nurse can assess' accurately reflects this.
claims.limitations: On-the-day clinical judgement required.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate and safely hedged. No change needed.

claims.page_title: Childhood Immunisations and Development Checks With a GP
claims.claim_text: Seek urgent care for breathing difficulty, a baby under three months with fever, a child who is very drowsy or floppy, a non-blanching rash, dehydration, a seizure, severe allergic reaction or if your instinct says your child is seriously unwell.
claims.recommended_wording: Call 000 for breathing difficulty, a seizure, a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), a non-blanching rash (one that does not fade when you press on it), or a child who is very drowsy, floppy or hard to wake. See a doctor urgently, on the same day, for a baby under three months with a fever (38C or higher), signs of dehydration, or if your instinct says your child is seriously unwell. If in doubt, it is always okay to seek help.

primary_source.title: Kids Health Info: Fever in children

supporting_source.title: Fever and high temperature in children and babies - when to see a doctor

claims.evidence_summary: All listed red flags are clinically correct. RCH advises calling an ambulance (000) for a child struggling to breathe/blue/pale, a first seizure or a seizure over five minutes or one after which the child does not wake, and going to hospital for a non-blanching rash or a baby under one month with fever, and seeing a doctor for a baby under three months with fever. Grouping the most time-critical signs (breathing difficulty, seizure, anaphylaxis, non-blanching rash, unrousable/floppy child) under an explicit 'call 000' instruction, and the rest under 'same-day doctor', makes the advice safer and matches RCH. The article's conservative treatment of under-3-months fever as urgent is appropriate.
claims.limitations: Educational; not a substitute for assessment.
claims.reviewer_notes: Facts correct but the single 'seek urgent care' verb blurs 000-level from same-day-GP-level emergencies. Split as recommended. Consider adding fever threshold (38C) for the under-3-months trigger, consistent with RCH. [Implemented 2026-09-20; applied to site - see corresponding IND entry.]

claims.page_title: Starting Solids and Allergy Foods: Calm Advice for Parents
claims.claim_text: Current Australian advice generally supports introducing solids when a baby is developmentally ready, around six months but not before four months, while continuing breastfeeding if possible.

primary_source.title: ASCIA Guideline: Infant Feeding for Food Allergy Prevention

supporting_source.title: How to Introduce Solid Foods to Babies

claims.evidence_summary: The updated ASCIA Guideline (published January 2026) states solids should be introduced when the baby shows signs of developmental readiness, usually around 6 months and not before 4 months, and that breastfeeding should continue if possible while introducing solids. The article's wording matches the current guideline almost verbatim.
claims.limitations: Timing individualised for some babies; article correctly adds 'some babies need individual advice'.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate and current (verified against the Jan 2026 ASCIA update). No change needed.

claims.page_title: Starting Solids and Allergy Foods: Calm Advice for Parents
claims.claim_text: Allergenic foods are usually introduced in age-appropriate forms during the first year, but some babies need individual advice.

primary_source.title: ASCIA Guideline: Infant Feeding for Food Allergy Prevention

claims.evidence_summary: ASCIA recommends introducing all common allergenic foods (including well-cooked egg and smooth peanut butter/paste, dairy, wheat) in age-appropriate forms in the first year of life (by 12 months), which reduces the risk of food allergy. The article's wording is accurate, and appropriately notes some babies need individual advice.
claims.limitations: High-risk infants (severe eczema, existing food allergy) may need medical guidance first - covered separately in the article.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate and current. No change needed.

claims.claim_text: Should allergy foods be delayed? For most babies, delaying common allergy foods is not recommended.

primary_source.title: ASCIA Guideline: Infant Feeding for Food Allergy Prevention

supporting_source.title: How to Introduce Solid Foods to Babies

claims.evidence_summary: ASCIA explicitly advises NOT delaying introduction of allergenic foods, as introducing them in the first year reduces allergy risk; the 2026 update encourages introducing well-cooked egg and peanut soon after starting solids. The article's wording is accurate and aligns with the strongest current evidence.
claims.limitations: Applies to most babies; high-risk infants need individual advice (covered elsewhere in article).
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate and current. No change needed.

claims.page_title: Starting Solids and Allergy Foods: Calm Advice for Parents
claims.claim_text: What is gagging versus choking? Gagging is noisy and part of learning textures. Choking may be silent or associated with inability to breathe, cough or cry, and requires urgent action.
claims.evidence_summary: Consistent with authoritative first-aid guidance: gagging is a normal, often noisy protective reflex as babies learn textures, whereas choking (airway obstruction) may be silent or show inability to breathe, cry or cough effectively and needs immediate first aid. Accurate and safety-appropriate.
claims.limitations: Educational; parents should learn infant choking first aid (e.g. via an accredited course).
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate. Optional enhancement: add 'call 000 and start back blows/chest thrusts if your baby is choking'. Not required for accuracy.

claims.page_title: Starting Solids and Allergy Foods: Calm Advice for Parents
claims.claim_text: Call 000 for signs of anaphylaxis such as breathing difficulty, swelling of the tongue or throat, collapse, persistent dizziness or a severe widespread reaction. Seek prompt medical care for repeated vomiting, poor feeding, dehydration, blood in stools or poor weight gain.

primary_source.title: ASCIA First Aid Plan for Anaphylaxis / signs of anaphylaxis

claims.evidence_summary: ASCIA lists signs of anaphylaxis including difficult/noisy breathing, swelling of the tongue, swelling/tightness in the throat, persistent dizziness or collapse, and (in young children) pale and floppy appearance, and directs to call an ambulance (000) and give adrenaline. The article's anaphylaxis red flags and 000 instruction match ASCIA. The additional 'seek prompt care' signs (repeated vomiting, poor feeding, dehydration, blood in stools, poor weight gain) are appropriate escalation triggers.
claims.limitations: Educational; families with known allergy should have an ASCIA Action Plan and adrenaline device.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate and correctly triaged to 000. No change needed.

claims.claim_text: For babies with severe eczema or previous reactions, the plan may need to be more cautious and coordinated. ... Can a GP help with eczema before solids? Yes. Improving eczema control can make feeding and allergy planning easier.

primary_source.title: ASCIA Guideline: Infant Feeding for Food Allergy Prevention

claims.evidence_summary: ASCIA identifies infants with severe eczema and/or existing food allergy as higher risk and recommends they still introduce allergenic foods in the first year but may need medical advice/individualised plans before doing so. Managing eczema is part of good allergy-prevention care. The article's cautious, coordinated approach for these infants is accurate and safe, and correctly does NOT advise blanket delay or avoidance.
claims.limitations: High-risk infants should be individually assessed; article appropriately signposts GP involvement.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate and safe. No change needed.

claims.page_title: Men's Health Checks in the Eastern Suburbs: What to Ask Your GP
claims.claim_text: Prostate screening is individual and should include a discussion of benefits, limitations and possible harms rather than a one-size-fits-all test. ... Should I have a prostate test? That decision should be individual. A GP can explain PSA testing, limitations and when further assessment is needed.

primary_source.title: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice (Red Book) - prostate cancer / PSA

supporting_source.title: Shared decision making in prostate cancer screening

claims.evidence_summary: The RACGP position is that PSA testing is not recommended as routine population screening of asymptomatic men; where a man requests it, the GP should support an informed, shared decision covering benefits, limitations and harms (overdiagnosis/overtreatment). The article's framing - individual, shared decision, harms included, 'not one-size-fits-all' - is exactly the current mainstream Australian position and does NOT promote routine screening.
claims.limitations: Guidance is contested internationally; some bodies differ. Australian position (RACGP; also RACGP/PSA testing pathway with Cancer Council Australia) is well represented here.
claims.reviewer_notes: CONTESTED WATCH ITEM cleared: balanced, benefit/harm framing present, no overstatement of screening benefit. Model example of safe wording. No change.

claims.limitations: Fertility outcomes depend on age, ovulatory status, BMI and other factors; a general page cannot individualise prognosis.
claims.reviewer_notes: Suggested minor addition keeps the warm, reassuring first-person-clinic voice while adding balancing context so the reassurance is not read as 'PCOS does not affect fertility'. en-AU, hyphens. Not an AHPRA guarantee issue as phrased, but the added nuance reduces the chance a patient delays fertility assessment. [Implemented 2026-09-20; applied to site - see corresponding IND entry.]

claims.page_title: Breast Lumps, Breast Pain and Screening: When to See a GP
claims.claim_text: screening mammograms are for people without symptoms. A new lump or change needs diagnostic assessment, not just routine screening.
claims.evidence_summary: BreastScreen is an asymptomatic screening program; symptomatic patients require diagnostic assessment (triple test) rather than screening. This distinction is central to safe care-seeking and is correctly stated.
claims.limitations: Care-affecting claim: correctly steers symptomatic patients away from screening-only pathways toward diagnostic assessment. This reduces, rather than creates, harm.
claims.reviewer_notes: Strong, defensible wording. This is the safest framing and should be preserved.

claims.page_title: Breast Lumps, Breast Pain and Screening: When to See a GP
claims.claim_text: The BreastScreen Australia Program targets women aged 50 to 74, while some others may be eligible.

supporting_source.org: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
supporting_source.title: Who should have a breast screen

claims.evidence_summary: Verified current: BreastScreen Australia actively invites women aged 50-74 for free 2-yearly mammograms; women aged 40-49 and 75+ are eligible for free screening but are not sent invitations. The article's 'targets 50 to 74, while some others may be eligible' is accurate and does not overstate.
claims.limitations: Program ages can change; verify at each review. The article correctly signals 'ask your GP what applies to you', avoiding an absolute eligibility claim.
claims.reviewer_notes: Dept of Health page (supporting_source) returned HTTP 503 on direct fetch on the verification date; content confirmed via Cancer Council Australia (which mirrors the program) and via search snapshot of the Dept page. Re-verify the Dept URL resolves at next review. This is a change-prone program rule - keep the 12-month review cadence.

claims.page_title: Cervical Screening and Self-Collection: A GP Guide for Patients
claims.claim_text: In Australia, routine screening looks for HPV, the virus that causes most cervical cancers.
claims.evidence_summary: The renewed National Cervical Screening Program uses a primary HPV test; HPV is described by Cancer Council as 'the main cause of cervical cancer' (persistent oncogenic HPV underlies almost all cases). 'Causes most cervical cancers' is accurate and conservatively worded.
claims.limitations: 'Most' is a conservative phrasing (HPV is implicated in ~99% of cases); no overstatement.
claims.reviewer_notes: No change needed.

claims.page_title: Cervical Screening and Self-Collection: A GP Guide for Patients
claims.claim_text: The National Cervical Screening Program invites women and people with a cervix aged 25 to 74 to have a Cervical Screening Test every five years through a healthcare provider.

supporting_source.org: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
supporting_source.title: About the National Cervical Screening Program

claims.evidence_summary: Verified current: eligible people aged 25-74 with a cervix are invited to a 5-yearly HPV-based Cervical Screening Test. Ages and interval match the program exactly.
claims.limitations: Change-prone program rule; verify ages/interval each review. Dept of Health page returned HTTP 503 on direct fetch; confirmed via Cancer Council Australia and search snapshot.
claims.reviewer_notes: Re-verify the Dept URL resolves at next review. Keep 12-month cadence for this program rule.

claims.page_title: Cervical Screening and Self-Collection: A GP Guide for Patients
claims.claim_text: Many eligible patients can now choose self-collection ... Eligible patients can collect their own vaginal sample in a private space after instructions from a healthcare provider.

supporting_source.org: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
supporting_source.title: Self-collection for cervical screening

claims.evidence_summary: Since 1 July 2022 self-collection of a vaginal sample has been available to all screen-eligible people aged 25-74 who choose it, accessed through a healthcare provider; it is as effective at detecting HPV as a clinician-collected sample. Article wording ('many eligible patients', 'after instructions from a healthcare provider') is accurate.
claims.limitations: The article correctly notes eligibility and that self-collection is arranged via a provider; it does not overstate universal availability without provider involvement.
claims.reviewer_notes: Consider (optional) adding that self-collection is now offered to all screening participants who choose it, not only a subset - current 'many eligible patients' slightly understates availability but is not incorrect. No change required. Dept of Health self-collection page returned 503 on direct fetch; corroborated by Cancer Council and search snapshot.

claims.page_title: Cervical Screening and Self-Collection: A GP Guide for Patients
claims.claim_text: Do I need screening if I have had the HPV vaccine? Yes. HPV vaccination reduces risk but does not replace cervical screening.
claims.evidence_summary: Cancer Council states 'whether you've had the HPV vaccine or not, regular screening remains essential'. The claim is accurate and important for safe care-seeking.
claims.limitations: None material.
claims.reviewer_notes: No change needed - this is a key safety message.

claims.page_title: Cervical Screening and Self-Collection: A GP Guide for Patients
claims.claim_text: Screening is for people without symptoms. If you have symptoms such as bleeding after sex, bleeding between periods, pelvic pain or unusual discharge, you should book a GP review even if you are not due for routine screening.
claims.evidence_summary: Consistent with program guidance that screening is for asymptomatic people and that symptomatic presentations (especially postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding) need separate assessment. This is a key safety message and is correctly stated.
claims.limitations: None; strongly protective wording.
claims.reviewer_notes: Preserve on any future edit.

claims.page_title: Contraception Options in Australia: How a GP Can Help You Choose
claims.claim_text: Long-acting reversible methods such as implants and IUDs are among the most effective because they do not rely on daily remembering.
claims.evidence_summary: LARCs (implant and IUDs) are the most effective reversible methods (>99% effective) precisely because they remove reliance on daily user action ('set and forget'). The article's 'among the most effective because they do not rely on daily remembering' is accurate and, helpfully, avoids quoting bare percentages.
claims.limitations: No 'typical use vs perfect use' distinction is needed here because the claim is qualitative and correctly attributes effectiveness to independence from daily adherence. If a numeric figure is ever added, it must be labelled and given with typical-use context.
claims.reviewer_notes: Good practice - the article states relative effectiveness without unqualified numbers. If future edits add percentages, flag for typical-use qualification.

claims.page_title: Contraception Options in Australia: How a GP Can Help You Choose
claims.claim_text: Contraception prevents pregnancy, but most methods do not protect against STIs.
claims.evidence_summary: healthdirect states condoms are the only contraceptive method that also helps prevent STIs; all hormonal and intrauterine methods provide no STI protection. 'Most methods do not protect against STIs' is accurate.
claims.limitations: None; important safety message.
claims.reviewer_notes: No change needed.

claims.page_title: Implanon and IUD Questions: What to Ask Your GP Before Choosing
claims.claim_text: Hormonal IUD: A device placed inside the uterus that releases hormone and can reduce bleeding for many people.
claims.evidence_summary: The hormonal (levonorgestrel) IUD reduces menstrual bleeding for many users and is used to manage heavy menstrual bleeding. 'Can reduce bleeding for many people' is accurate and appropriately hedged.
claims.limitations: None; 'can ... for many people' avoids over-promising a universal effect.
claims.reviewer_notes: No change needed.

claims.page_title: Implanon and IUD Questions: What to Ask Your GP Before Choosing
claims.claim_text: Copper IUD: A non-hormonal intrauterine device that can also be used for emergency contraception in some circumstances.
claims.evidence_summary: The copper IUD is non-hormonal and can be used as emergency contraception when inserted within the recommended window (about 5 days) after unprotected sex. 'In some circumstances' correctly reflects the timing/eligibility limits.
claims.limitations: None; appropriately qualified.
claims.reviewer_notes: No change needed.

claims.page_title: Implanon and IUD Questions: What to Ask Your GP Before Choosing
claims.claim_text: Will an implant or IUD affect future fertility? Fertility usually returns after removal, although timing can vary.
claims.evidence_summary: Fertility returns rapidly after removal of the implant or IUD, with normal return to baseline fertility; timing of the first ovulation/cycle can vary between individuals. 'Usually returns ... timing can vary' is accurate and appropriately non-absolute.
claims.limitations: None; correctly avoids guaranteeing an outcome or timeframe.
claims.reviewer_notes: No change needed.

claims.page_title: Implanon and IUD Questions: What to Ask Your GP Before Choosing
claims.claim_text: Can a hormonal IUD help heavy periods? For many people it can reduce bleeding, but suitability depends on the cause of bleeding and your medical history.
claims.evidence_summary: The levonorgestrel IUD is an established first-line treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding and reduces bleeding for many users. Wording is accurate and correctly conditions suitability on cause and history.
claims.limitations: None; appropriately hedged.
claims.reviewer_notes: No change needed.

claims.page_title: Implanon and IUD Questions: What to Ask Your GP Before Choosing
claims.claim_text: Do I still need condoms? Condoms are still important for STI protection ... because implants and IUDs do not protect against STIs.
claims.evidence_summary: Implants and IUDs provide no STI protection; condoms remain necessary for STI risk reduction. Accurate and an important safety message.
claims.limitations: None.
claims.reviewer_notes: No change needed.

claims.page_title: Sexual Health, Vaginal Symptoms and STI Testing: A GP Visit Should Feel Safe
claims.claim_text: Can I have an STI without symptoms? Yes. Many STIs can be silent, so testing can be useful after new partners or possible exposure.
claims.evidence_summary: healthdirect confirms you can have an STI without noticing symptoms and that testing may be recommended even without symptoms (e.g. after a new partner). Many STIs (notably chlamydia) are frequently asymptomatic. Accurate.
claims.limitations: None; important care-seeking message.
claims.reviewer_notes: No change needed.

claims.page_title: ADHD Concerns in Children: First Steps With a GP
claims.claim_text: ADHD assessment is not based on one behaviour or one bad term at school. Sleep problems, anxiety, learning difficulties, hearing or vision issues, trauma, family stress, autism, giftedness, medication effects and other health concerns can overlap.

primary_source.title: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

supporting_source.title: Kids Health Info: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)

claims.evidence_summary: The Australian ADHD Guideline requires diagnosis to be based on comprehensive assessment of persistent symptoms causing functional impairment across settings, with explicit consideration and exclusion of differential/co-occurring conditions (sleep disorders, anxiety, learning disorders, sensory deficits, trauma, autism). This directly supports the article's message that ADHD is not diagnosed from a single behaviour and that overlapping causes must be considered.
claims.limitations: General educational statement; individual assessment still required.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate and appropriately cautious. No change needed.

claims.page_title: ADHD Concerns in Children: First Steps With a GP
claims.claim_text: Could sleep problems look like ADHD? Yes. Poor sleep, snoring and tiredness can affect concentration and behaviour, so sleep should be discussed.

primary_source.title: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

supporting_source.title: Sleep and children: how sleep affects behaviour and learning

claims.evidence_summary: Sleep disturbance (including sleep-disordered breathing/snoring/obstructive sleep apnoea) is a well-recognised mimic of, and contributor to, inattention and hyperactivity in children, and the guideline recommends assessing sleep as part of ADHD assessment. Statement is accurate.
claims.limitations: General; sleep is one of several factors to assess.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate. No change needed.

claims.page_title: Baby and Childhood Eczema: Getting the Basics Right
claims.claim_text: Eczema is usually a skin barrier problem, not a sign that a parent has done something wrong. It can be worsened by heat, soaps, saliva, infections, scratching, irritants and sometimes allergy.
claims.evidence_summary: RCH and ASCIA describe eczema as a chronic condition involving a defective skin barrier and inflammation, aggravated by triggers including heat, soap/irritants, dryness, infection, scratching, saliva and sometimes allergens. Statement is accurate and appropriately reassuring.
claims.limitations: General; causes are multifactorial.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate. No change needed.

claims.page_title: Baby and Childhood Eczema: Getting the Basics Right
claims.claim_text: Under-treating inflammation can sometimes prolong the flare and increase scratching.
claims.evidence_summary: Guidelines emphasise treating flares adequately and early with topical corticosteroids of appropriate strength, and note that under-use (often driven by steroid phobia) leads to poorly controlled, prolonged eczema and ongoing itch/scratch. Statement aligns with guidance.
claims.limitations: General; treatment intensity is individualised.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate and a useful counter to steroid phobia. No change needed.

claims.page_title: Baby and Childhood Eczema: Getting the Basics Right
claims.claim_text: How much moisturiser should I use? Often more than people expect. Regular generous moisturising helps repair the skin barrier.
claims.evidence_summary: RCH and ASCIA recommend frequent, generous use of emollients as the mainstay of eczema care to restore and maintain the skin barrier. Statement is accurate.
claims.limitations: General; product choice individualised.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate. No change needed.

claims.page_title: Baby and Childhood Eczema: Getting the Basics Right
claims.claim_text: Infected eczema: Eczema complicated by bacteria or viruses, often causing pain, crusting, weeping or fever.
claims.evidence_summary: Consistent with RCH: infected eczema may be bacterial (commonly Staphylococcus aureus - weeping, crusting, pain) or viral (herpes simplex/eczema herpeticum), sometimes with fever. Accurate definition.
claims.limitations: Plain-language summary.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate. No change needed.

claims.page_title: Childhood Immunisations and Development Checks With a GP
claims.claim_text: Catch-up schedule: A plan to safely update missed or delayed vaccines. ... Catch-up schedules should be tailored to the child's age and vaccine history.

primary_source.org: Australian Government Department of Health (Australian Immunisation Handbook)
primary_source.title: Catch-up vaccination

claims.evidence_summary: The Australian Immunisation Handbook provides catch-up schedules individualised by the person's age, doses already received and interval requirements. The article's statement accurately reflects that catch-up must be tailored to age and vaccine history.
claims.limitations: General; actual catch-up calculated per Handbook/state provider.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate. No change needed.

claims.page_title: Childhood Immunisations and Development Checks With a GP
claims.claim_text: What side effects are common after vaccines? Mild fever, tiredness, irritability or soreness can occur. Your GP should explain what is expected and what is not.

primary_source.org: Australian Government Department of Health (Australian Immunisation Handbook)
primary_source.title: After vaccination / adverse events following immunisation

claims.evidence_summary: Common expected reactions listed by the Handbook and Raising Children Network include low-grade fever, irritability, tiredness/drowsiness and local injection-site soreness/redness/swelling. Accurate.
claims.limitations: General; specific reactions vary by vaccine.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate. No change needed.

claims.page_title: Childhood Immunisations and Development Checks With a GP
claims.claim_text: Milestones: Skills many children develop around certain ages, such as sitting, walking, talking and social interaction. ... development concerns (speech, movement, feeding, sleep, behaviour) are worth raising at a vaccine visit.

supporting_source.title: Child health checks / My Personal Health Record

claims.evidence_summary: Accurate plain-language description of developmental milestones; aligns with Raising Children Network and the schedule of child health/development checks. Encouraging parents to raise concerns early is consistent with best-practice developmental surveillance.
claims.limitations: Milestones are ranges, not fixed ages; article correctly says 'around certain ages'.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate. No change needed.

claims.page_title: Starting Solids and Allergy Foods: Calm Advice for Parents
claims.claim_text: Allergenic foods: Foods such as egg, peanut, dairy, wheat, fish and others that commonly cause allergy.

primary_source.title: ASCIA Guideline: Infant Feeding for Food Allergy Prevention

claims.evidence_summary: ASCIA lists the most common allergy-causing foods as cow's milk (dairy), egg, peanut, tree nuts, wheat, soy, sesame, fish and shellfish. The article's examples are a correct subset ('and others' covers the rest). Accurate.
claims.limitations: Illustrative list, not exhaustive; article says 'and others'.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate. Optional: could add tree nuts, soy, sesame, shellfish for completeness. Not required.

claims.page_title: Starting Solids and Allergy Foods: Calm Advice for Parents
claims.claim_text: Iron-rich foods are important early. The exact first food is less important than safe texture, variety over time and responsive feeding.

primary_source.title: How to Introduce Solid Foods to Babies

claims.evidence_summary: ASCIA and the NHMRC Infant Feeding Guidelines recommend iron-rich foods (e.g. iron-fortified cereals, pureed meat, well-cooked legumes) as among the first foods because infant iron stores decline around 6 months. Emphasis on texture progression, variety and responsive feeding is consistent with guidance. Accurate.
claims.limitations: General nutrition advice.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate. No change needed.

claims.page_title: Starting Solids and Allergy Foods: Calm Advice for Parents
claims.claim_text: They can discuss ... safe forms of peanut and egg, choking hazards ...

primary_source.title: How to Introduce Solid Foods to Babies

supporting_source.title: Choking: first aid and prevention / safe foods for babies

claims.evidence_summary: ASCIA advises giving allergenic foods in safe forms (e.g. smooth peanut butter/paste rather than whole nuts, well-cooked egg) and avoiding choking hazards such as whole nuts, hard/round foods for infants. Accurate.
claims.limitations: General.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate. No change needed.

claims.page_title: Acne Treatment for Teens and Adults: When to See a GP
claims.claim_text: Early treatment can reduce scarring and months of frustration. ... Sometimes, but waiting can increase scarring risk.
claims.evidence_summary: Delayed or inadequate treatment of inflammatory/cystic acne is a recognised risk factor for permanent scarring; earlier effective treatment reduces that risk. The copy already uses proportionate 'can reduce'/'can increase' language rather than absolute claims.
claims.limitations: Scarring risk is individual and depends on acne type and severity; benefit of 'early' treatment is supported directionally rather than by a single quantified figure.
claims.reviewer_notes: Wording is proportionate and defensible. No change needed.

claims.page_title: Acne Treatment for Teens and Adults: When to See a GP
claims.claim_text: Acne treatment usually needs patience. Many options take 8 to 12 weeks to show clear improvement, and some can irritate skin at first if started too quickly.
claims.evidence_summary: Standard dermatology guidance is that acne treatments (topical retinoids, topical/oral antibiotics) commonly take 8-12 weeks or longer before clear improvement is seen, and topical retinoids often cause initial irritation. The 8-12 week figure aligns with authoritative sources.
claims.limitations: Timeframe is a general expectation; some regimens take longer than 12 weeks.
claims.reviewer_notes: Specific numeric claim verified. Acceptable.

claims.page_title: Acne Treatment for Teens and Adults: When to See a GP
claims.claim_text: Retinoid: A vitamin A related acne treatment; some forms are not safe in pregnancy. ... referral for isotretinoin when acne is severe, scarring or resistant ... what to avoid in pregnancy.
claims.evidence_summary: Oral isotretinoin is a known teratogen with strict pregnancy-prevention requirements; topical retinoids are generally avoided/cautioned in pregnancy. The article's cautious framing ('some forms are not safe in pregnancy', 'strict safety rules') is accurate and appropriately non-alarming.
claims.limitations: Exact pregnancy-category advice varies by agent; correctly deferred to the GP.
claims.reviewer_notes: Safety framing is accurate and proportionate.

claims.page_title: Eczema, Psoriasis and Chronic Skin Conditions: Getting a GP Plan
claims.claim_text: Used correctly, topical steroids can be very helpful and safe. Problems are more likely when they are the wrong strength, used in the wrong place, or used without a plan.
claims.evidence_summary: Topical corticosteroids used at appropriate potency, site and duration are effective and safe for eczema; adverse effects are associated with inappropriate strength/site/duration. The reassurance is correctly conditioned on correct use, addressing common steroid-phobia without dismissing risk.
claims.limitations: Safety is conditional on correct use, which the copy states.
claims.reviewer_notes: Balanced. Reassurance is qualified. Acceptable.

claims.page_title: Eczema, Psoriasis and Chronic Skin Conditions: Getting a GP Plan
claims.claim_text: Can psoriasis affect more than skin? Yes. It can be associated with joint inflammation and other health risks ... your GP may also ask about joint pain, nails and cardiovascular risk.

supporting_source.org: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
supporting_source.title: Cardiovascular Risk in Patients With Psoriasis: JACC Review

claims.evidence_summary: Psoriasis is associated with psoriatic arthritis (joint inflammation) and with increased cardiovascular risk driven by chronic inflammation and shared risk factors. The 'can be associated with' phrasing is exactly the correct (association, not causation) framing.
claims.limitations: Absolute CV risk elevation is greatest in severe disease; the article does not quantify, which is appropriate for general information.
claims.reviewer_notes: Uses 'associated with' correctly. Model wording. No change.

claims.page_title: Family GP Care in Maroubra: Why Continuity Matters
claims.claim_text: A regular family GP can help join these pieces together ... Continuity ... means there is a trusted place to return to ... For adults, it helps with screening, mental health, lifestyle change and long-term risk reduction.

primary_source.org: British Journal of General Practice (Pereira Gray et al.)
primary_source.title: Primary medical care continuity and patient mortality: a systematic review

claims.evidence_summary: Systematic-review evidence (Pereira Gray 2018/2020) links higher continuity of care with better outcomes and lower all-cause mortality across multiple countries, and RACGP endorses continuity. IMPORTANTLY, this article does NOT make the contested strong claim ('continuity reduces mortality'); it stays with proportionate benefits (joined-up care, screening, risk reduction). This is the safe position.
claims.limitations: The mortality evidence is observational (cohort/cross-sectional), so causation is not proven - which is why the article's avoidance of a mortality claim is appropriate. Do NOT add a 'reduces mortality' claim to this copy.
claims.reviewer_notes: WATCH ITEM cleared: copy does not overstate. If future edits add 'continuity reduces mortality', downgrade to 'is associated with lower mortality in observational studies' and cite Pereira Gray.

claims.page_title: GP, Urgent Care or 000? How to Decide in Sydney's Eastern Suburbs
claims.claim_text: 000: Australia's emergency number for ambulance, police or fire. ... If your condition deteriorates while waiting, do not drive yourself; contact emergency services instead.
claims.evidence_summary: 000 is correctly described as the Australian emergency number for ambulance, police and fire. 'Do not drive yourself, call emergency services' is standard, correct safety advice for a deteriorating patient (e.g. suspected cardiac/stroke).
claims.limitations: None material.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate and safe.

claims.page_title: How to Choose a GP in Sydney's Eastern Suburbs
claims.claim_text: Dr Amanda Henderson is a local GP at GP Maroubra who provides caring, family-focused general practice close to home. ... What makes a good GP for a family? Look for someone who listens carefully, explains clearly, keeps good follow-up systems ...

primary_source.title: Advertising a regulated health service - guidelines

claims.evidence_summary: Self-description uses non-comparative, verifiable language ('caring, family-focused general practice'). There is NO 'best GP', superiority, or comparative claim, and no patient testimonials, so it does not trigger the main AHPRA s.133 advertising prohibitions. Qualities are framed as general 'what to look for' advice, not exclusive claims.
claims.limitations: AHPRA compliance is a regulatory matter, not a clinical evidence question; no legal conclusion is offered here.
claims.reviewer_notes: Regulatory scan: no superiority/testimonial red flags found on this page. 'Caring/family-focused' is acceptable descriptive language.

claims.page_title: How to Choose a GP in Sydney's Eastern Suburbs
claims.claim_text: It is much easier to get good care when you have a regular doctor or practice that knows your background. Continuity matters for pregnancy planning, children's health, mental health, chronic conditions, contraception, preventive screening ...

supporting_source.org: British Journal of General Practice (Pereira Gray et al.)
supporting_source.title: Primary medical care continuity and patient mortality: a systematic review

claims.evidence_summary: Continuity of care is associated with better preventive care uptake, chronic disease management and patient outcomes. 'Easier to get good care' is a proportionate, non-absolute benefit statement.
claims.limitations: Observational evidence base (see GEN-10 limitations).
claims.reviewer_notes: Acceptable; no mortality overstatement.

claims.page_title: Lifestyle Medicine: Weight, Sleep, Alcohol, Smoking and Wellbeing
claims.claim_text: Sleep apnoea: Interrupted breathing during sleep, often linked with snoring, tiredness and cardiometabolic risk.

primary_source.title: Caffeine, Food, Alcohol, Smoking and Sleep / OSA resources

claims.evidence_summary: Obstructive sleep apnoea involves interrupted breathing during sleep, is associated with snoring and daytime tiredness, and untreated OSA is linked to cardiovascular/cardiometabolic risk. 'Often linked with' is correctly associational.
claims.limitations: None material; definition is accurate.
claims.reviewer_notes: WATCH ITEM cleared. Uses 'linked with', not 'causes'. Acceptable.

claims.page_title: Lifestyle Medicine: Weight, Sleep, Alcohol, Smoking and Wellbeing
claims.claim_text: Can alcohol affect sleep even if it helps me fall asleep? Yes. Alcohol can fragment sleep and worsen snoring, reflux, mood and blood pressure.

primary_source.title: Caffeine, Food, Alcohol, Smoking and Sleep

supporting_source.title: Australian Guidelines to Reduce Health Risks from Drinking Alcohol

claims.evidence_summary: Sleep Health Foundation states alcohol may help falling asleep but disrupts sleep architecture causing fragmented sleep, and even modest amounts increase snoring and OSA frequency/intensity; alcohol also worsens reflux, mood and blood pressure. Fully supported.
claims.limitations: Effect size varies with dose and individual; article gives no numeric guideline (so no NHMRC-number discrepancy risk).
claims.reviewer_notes: WATCH ITEM cleared. Accurate. Note: page does not quote specific NHMRC standard-drink limits, so no guideline-figure exposure.

claims.page_title: Lifestyle Medicine: Weight, Sleep, Alcohol, Smoking and Wellbeing
claims.claim_text: Sleep is poor and affecting mood, energy or concentration. ... [reasons to book]
claims.evidence_summary: Poor sleep is bidirectionally associated with mood, energy and concentration, and can increase the risk of mood disorders (Sleep Health Foundation). Framed as a reason to seek help rather than a causal claim; proportionate.
claims.limitations: Relationship is bidirectional; article does not overclaim direction.
claims.reviewer_notes: WATCH ITEM (sleep->mood) cleared. Acceptable.

claims.page_title: Lifestyle Medicine: Weight, Sleep, Alcohol, Smoking and Wellbeing
claims.claim_text: You want to reduce heart, diabetes, liver, cancer or mental health risk. ... Is weight always just about calories? No. Sleep, hormones, medications, mental health, pain, environment, genetics and life stress can all affect weight.

primary_source.title: Healthy living / reducing heart disease risk

supporting_source.title: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice (Red Book) - lifestyle risk factors

claims.evidence_summary: Modifiable lifestyle factors (smoking, alcohol, diet, activity, weight) are established contributors to cardiovascular, diabetes, liver, several cancer and mental-health risks, and weight regulation is genuinely multifactorial. Framed as patient goals ('you want to reduce ... risk') using 'reduce risk' rather than 'prevent'. Proportionate.
claims.limitations: 'Reduce risk' is directional; no quantified risk reduction is claimed, which is appropriate.
claims.reviewer_notes: WATCH ITEM cleared. Uses 'reduce risk' correctly; multifactorial weight framing reduces stigma and is accurate.

claims.page_title: Lifestyle Medicine: Weight, Sleep, Alcohol, Smoking and Wellbeing
claims.claim_text: Can a GP prescribe medication for quitting smoking? Often yes ... Behavioural support and follow-up increase the chance of success.

primary_source.title: Supporting smoking cessation: A guide for health professionals

supporting_source.title: Combined pharmacotherapy and behavioural interventions for smoking cessation

claims.evidence_summary: Combining pharmacotherapy with behavioural support and follow-up increases smoking-cessation success versus minimal support (RACGP; Cochrane). 'Increase the chance of success' is accurate and proportionate.
claims.limitations: Suitability of pharmacotherapy is individual, which the copy states ('depending on your history and suitability').
claims.reviewer_notes: Acceptable.

claims.page_title: Men's Health Checks in the Eastern Suburbs: What to Ask Your GP
claims.claim_text: Bowel screening: Testing for hidden blood in stool for eligible people without symptoms. ... bowel cancer screening [as part of a men's health check].

primary_source.org: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
primary_source.title: National Bowel Cancer Screening Program

claims.evidence_summary: The NBCSP uses an immunochemical faecal occult blood test (iFOBT) to detect hidden blood in stool in eligible people WITHOUT symptoms (currently ages 45-74, free every 2 years). The definition is accurate; the article wisely does not quote an age that could go stale.
claims.limitations: Eligibility age changed to 45 from July 2024; article avoids stating an age so remains correct.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate. Optional enhancement: could note the program is for ages 45-74, but current wording is safe.

claims.page_title: Men's Health Checks in the Eastern Suburbs: What to Ask Your GP
claims.claim_text: Cardiovascular risk: The chance of heart attack or stroke based on factors such as age, blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking and diabetes.

primary_source.org: Australian Government / Australian Chronic Disease Prevention Alliance
primary_source.title: Australian CVD risk assessment guideline (cvdcheck.org.au)

claims.evidence_summary: Australian CVD risk assessment estimates the probability of a heart attack or stroke from age, sex, blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking status and diabetes. Definition is accurate.
claims.limitations: Full risk calculators include additional variables; article gives a fair lay summary.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate.

claims.page_title: Preventive Health Checks for Busy Adults
claims.claim_text: Screening: Testing offered to people without symptoms when evidence supports benefit. ... Not every test is useful for every person; unnecessary testing can create confusion as well as reassurance.

primary_source.title: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice (Red Book)

claims.evidence_summary: The RACGP Red Book frames screening as appropriate only where evidence supports net benefit, and explicitly warns against low-value/unnecessary testing (false positives, overdiagnosis). The article's definition and its acknowledgement of harms of over-testing align precisely with this evidence-based framing.
claims.limitations: None material.
claims.reviewer_notes: WATCH ITEM (screening benefit) cleared: benefit AND harms both acknowledged. Exemplary framing.

claims.page_title: Preventive Health Checks for Busy Adults
claims.claim_text: Are full body scans useful for prevention? Usually not as a routine screening tool. A GP can explain which evidence-based checks are more useful for your risk.

primary_source.title: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice (Red Book)

claims.evidence_summary: Routine whole-body scanning of asymptomatic people is not recommended (risk of false positives, incidentalomas, radiation, overdiagnosis) and is discouraged by RACGP and Choosing Wisely Australia. The article's 'usually not as a routine screening tool' is accurate.

claims.page_title: Women's Health GP in Maroubra | Dr Amanda Henderson

claims.category: clinical / menstrual health (when to seek care)

claims.limitations: General guidance; individual assessment still required.

claims.page_title: Women's Health GP in Maroubra | Dr Amanda Henderson
claims.claim_text: Can a GP help with low iron and iron deficiency? claims.evidence_summary: Healthdirect confirms iron deficiency is the most common nutritional disorder, that heavy periods are a common cause of blood loss, that it is diagnosed by an iron study blood test (ferritin is a component), and that treatment ranges from diet to iron tablets to IV iron infusion for severe deficiency, with treatment depending on the underlying cause. Symptoms including tiredness, breathlessness and light-headedness/faintness are listed.
