claims.reviewer_notes: Well qualified. No change needed.

claims.page_title: When Should I See a GP Before Trying for a Baby?
claims.claim_text: If you or your partner have a family history of inherited conditions, or if you are from a higher-risk background for certain genetic conditions, your GP can discuss genetic carrier screening and referral options.
claims.evidence_summary: GP discussion of reproductive/genetic carrier screening is appropriate; since Nov 2023 a Medicare-funded three-condition carrier screen (CF, SMA, fragile X) is available to all couples, with expanded panels for higher-risk backgrounds. Article's wording (offered to those with family history or higher-risk background) is accurate, if slightly narrower than current universal-offer availability.
claims.limitations: Universal three-condition carrier screening is now offered to all couples, not only higher-risk ones; article is not wrong but could optionally mention screening is available to anyone who wishes it. Not a safety issue.
claims.reviewer_notes: Optional enhancement only: could note carrier screening is available to all couples via Medicare, not just higher-risk backgrounds. No safety concern.

claims.page_title: When Should I See a GP Before Trying for a Baby?
claims.claim_text: If you are pregnant or might be pregnant, seek urgent medical care if you have: heavy vaginal bleeding, severe abdominal or pelvic pain, shoulder tip pain, fainting ... severe one-sided pelvic pain, fever with pelvic pain, severe vomiting and inability to keep fluids down, thoughts of harming yourself or feeling unsafe.
claims.evidence_summary: Correctly captures ectopic/early-pregnancy emergency signs (one-sided pain, shoulder-tip pain, syncope, heavy bleeding), hyperemesis, pelvic infection and acute mental health risk. Accurate.
claims.limitations: None material.
claims.reviewer_notes: No change needed.

claims.page_title: When Should I See a GP Before Trying for a Baby?
claims.claim_text: Can a GP check if I am fertile? A GP can assess factors that may affect fertility, such as cycle regularity, age, medical history, medications, and previous conditions. If needed, your GP can organise initial tests or refer you to a fertility specialist.
claims.evidence_summary: Correctly avoids implying a GP can 'confirm fertility'; instead states a GP can assess contributing factors and arrange initial tests/referral. Accurate and appropriately modest.
claims.limitations: None material.
claims.reviewer_notes: Careful wording ('assess factors', not 'confirm you are fertile'). No change needed.

claims.page_title: Perimenopause and Menopause: Questions to Bring to Your GP
claims.claim_text: Hot flushes, night sweats, sleep disruption, mood changes, brain fog, joint aches, vaginal dryness, low libido and heavier or more irregular periods can all affect quality of life.
claims.evidence_summary: Australian sources list hot flushes, night sweats, sleep problems, mood changes, brain fog/concentration, joint aches, vaginal dryness, reduced libido and menstrual changes among recognised perimenopausal/menopausal symptoms. The claim is appropriately hedged ('can').
claims.limitations: Symptoms vary between individuals and some overlap with other conditions; the article correctly frames these as possible rather than universal.
claims.reviewer_notes: Well-hedged symptom list. No overstatement.

claims.page_title: Perimenopause and Menopause: Questions to Bring to Your GP
claims.claim_text: Blood tests are not always helpful in typical perimenopause, but they may be needed if symptoms are early, unusual or there are other concerns.
claims.evidence_summary: healthdirect states tests are usually not needed to confirm perimenopause, and that FSH testing may help mainly in women under 45. Australian/AMS guidance recommends FSH in women under 45 (and 40-45 with symptoms) but not routinely in women over 45 in the expected age range, because a single FSH is unreliable in the menopause transition.
claims.limitations: AMS information-sheet index URL used for the supporting source; the specific diagnosing-menopause sheet is behind the hub index. healthdirect fully supports the claim.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate and aligned with current Australian practice.

claims.page_title: Perimenopause and Menopause: Questions to Bring to Your GP
claims.claim_text: Do I need a blood test to diagnose menopause? Often no, especially in the usual age range with typical symptoms.
claims.evidence_summary: healthdirect confirms tests are usually not needed and FSH testing applies mainly to women under 45; for women in the expected age range (approximately 45-55) menopause is a clinical diagnosis based on age, symptoms and period changes.
claims.limitations: None material.
claims.reviewer_notes: Consistent with WHM-04. Accurate.

claims.page_title: Perimenopause and Menopause: Questions to Bring to Your GP
claims.claim_text: Do I still need contraception in perimenopause? Possibly. Periods can be irregular while ovulation still occurs. Ask your GP before stopping contraception.
claims.evidence_summary: healthdirect: 'You can still become pregnant until you reach menopause' and advises discussing contraception because ovulatory cycles can continue during perimenopause. The claim is accurate.
claims.limitations: None material.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate and safety-positive.

claims.page_title: Perimenopause and Menopause: Questions to Bring to Your GP
claims.claim_text: Can menopause affect mood and sleep? Yes. Hormonal changes, life stress and poor sleep can all interact.
claims.evidence_summary: Mood changes and sleep disturbance are recognised features of the menopause transition, with a multifactorial contribution from hormonal change, vasomotor symptoms, sleep disruption and life stressors. The article correctly frames these as interacting rather than purely hormonal.
claims.limitations: Causation is multifactorial; the article does not claim menopause causes clinical depression, which is appropriate.
claims.reviewer_notes: Well-hedged. No overstatement of a hormone-mood causal link.

claims.page_title: Understanding What Causes Heavy Periods
claims.claim_text: Heavy periods can be caused by many different things, including hormonal changes, fibroids, adenomyosis, endometriosis, polyps, thyroid problems, bleeding disorders, some medications, contraception changes, pregnancy-related issues, and changes around perimenopause.
claims.evidence_summary: healthdirect lists fibroids, polyps, endometrial hyperplasia, adenomyosis, endometriosis, endometrial cancer, PCOS, hypothyroidism, perimenopause, hormone-based medicines/contraception and bleeding disorders (e.g. von Willebrand disease) as causes of heavy periods - matching the article's list.
claims.limitations: The article's list is broad; each cause's likelihood varies by age and history, which the article acknowledges downstream.
claims.reviewer_notes: Comprehensive and accurate causal list.

claims.page_title: Understanding What Causes Heavy Periods
claims.claim_text: Adenomyosis is more common in women in their 30s and 40s, but it can occur at other ages too.
claims.evidence_summary: Adenomyosis most often presents in women in their 30s to 50s (classically 40s-50s), and is increasingly recognised in the 30s; it can occur at other ages. The article's 'more common in 30s and 40s, but can occur at other ages' is a reasonable and appropriately hedged statement.
claims.limitations: Peak prevalence is often cited as 40s-50s; the article's lower age framing slightly under-emphasises the 50s but is not misleading. No resolving Australian consumer page dedicated to adenomyosis age distribution was located; an international authoritative source is used.
claims.reviewer_notes: Adjacent list item 'pain that worsens over time' is a mild prognosis phrasing; consider softening to 'pain that may worsen over time' for consistency with the article's hedged voice.

claims.page_title: Understanding What Causes Heavy Periods
claims.claim_text: Endometriosis... is often associated with pain, but some people also experience heavy bleeding.
claims.evidence_summary: Endometriosis is predominantly associated with pain (dysmenorrhoea, pelvic pain, dyspareunia) and infertility; heavy/irregular bleeding occurs in some patients but is not a defining feature. The article correctly foregrounds pain and hedges heavy bleeding as occurring in 'some people'.
claims.limitations: Heavy bleeding in endometriosis may partly reflect co-existing adenomyosis or fibroids; the article's caution is appropriate.
claims.reviewer_notes: Correctly avoids over-attributing heavy bleeding to endometriosis.

claims.page_title: Understanding What Causes Heavy Periods
claims.claim_text: Heavy periods are a common cause of iron deficiency and anaemia.

supporting_source.title: Heavy menstrual bleeding and iron deficiency: breaking the vicious cycle

claims.evidence_summary: healthdirect: 'Blood loss from heavy periods can lower your levels of iron and red blood cells. This can cause iron deficiency and anaemia.' Heavy menstrual bleeding is described in the literature as the single most common cause of iron-deficiency anaemia in reproductive-age women. Fully supports the claim.
claims.limitations: None material.
claims.reviewer_notes: Well-established.

claims.page_title: Understanding What Causes Heavy Periods
claims.claim_text: An underactive or overactive thyroid may contribute to heavy periods, irregular periods, fatigue, weight changes, temperature sensitivity, mood changes, changes in hair or skin.
claims.evidence_summary: healthdirect lists hypothyroidism among causes of heavy periods; both hypo- and hyperthyroidism are recognised causes of menstrual disturbance and the systemic symptoms listed. The claim uses 'may contribute', which is appropriately hedged.
claims.limitations: Thyroid disease is a less common cause of HMB than structural/hormonal causes; the article correctly recommends a blood test rather than assuming thyroid cause.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate and hedged.

claims.page_title: Understanding What Causes Heavy Periods
claims.claim_text: Heavy or irregular bleeding can occur with... a copper intrauterine device... [and] some long-acting contraceptive methods, especially in the early months.
claims.evidence_summary: healthdirect lists hormone-based medicines/contraception among causes of altered bleeding. The copper IUD is well recognised to increase menstrual blood loss and cramping, and long-acting hormonal methods commonly cause irregular bleeding in early months. Consistent with established contraceptive counselling.
claims.limitations: The article does not distinguish copper (typically heavier) from hormonal IUD (typically lighter); this is clarified elsewhere in the cluster (hormonal IUD listed as a treatment to reduce bleeding).
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate. Note contrast with hormonal IUD as HMB treatment (WHM-19/WHM-24) is handled correctly elsewhere.

claims.page_title: Understanding What Causes Heavy Periods
claims.claim_text: Options may include: iron replacement if iron is low, anti-inflammatory medication for some people, non-hormonal medication to reduce bleeding, hormonal contraception, hormonal intrauterine device, treatment of thyroid or other medical conditions...

supporting_source.title: Clinical Practice Guidelines: Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding

claims.evidence_summary: Standard HMB management includes iron replacement, NSAIDs, tranexamic acid (non-hormonal antifibrinolytic), the combined pill/progestogens and the levonorgestrel IUD (often first-line), plus treating underlying causes - consistent with Australian and NICE guidance. The article uses 'may include', which is appropriately non-prescriptive.
claims.limitations: The article does not rank options; this is appropriate for general information deferring to individualised care.
claims.reviewer_notes: Educational description of treatment classes; no specific brand promotion (TGA-safe). Levonorgestrel IUS is commonly first-line - could be noted but not required.

claims.page_title: Understanding What Causes Heavy Periods
claims.claim_text: Your GP may recommend: pregnancy test, full blood count to check for anaemia, iron studies or ferritin, thyroid function test, cervical screening test if due, STI testing if relevant, pelvic ultrasound, further hormonal tests in selected cases...
claims.evidence_summary: Recommended investigations for HMB routinely include pregnancy test, full blood count, ferritin/iron studies, thyroid function where indicated, cervical screening if due, STI testing where relevant and pelvic ultrasound - consistent with Australian primary-care practice. The article appropriately states 'not everyone needs every test'.
claims.limitations: None material.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate, tailored framing.

claims.page_title: Heavy Periods and Iron Deficiency: How a GP Can Help
claims.claim_text: Iron deficiency: Low iron stores, which can cause fatigue even before anaemia is present.

supporting_source.title: Iron deficiency without anaemia: a diagnosis that matters

claims.evidence_summary: Iron deficiency without anaemia (low ferritin, normal haemoglobin) is well described and can cause fatigue, poor concentration and other symptoms because iron has roles beyond haemoglobin (muscle, brain, energy metabolism). The claim is supported.
claims.limitations: The strength of the fatigue-without-anaemia association varies between studies; the article uses 'can cause', which is appropriately hedged.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate; supports appropriate testing (ferritin, not haemoglobin alone).

claims.page_title: Heavy Periods and Iron Deficiency: How a GP Can Help
claims.claim_text: Can low iron happen even if haemoglobin is normal? Yes. Iron stores can be low before anaemia develops, and symptoms can still occur.

primary_source.title: Iron deficiency without anaemia: a diagnosis that matters

claims.evidence_summary: Iron deficiency without anaemia (low ferritin with normal haemoglobin) is common and can be symptomatic; ferritin is the key test to detect it. Fully supports the claim and encourages appropriate testing.
claims.limitations: Ferritin can be falsely normal/raised as an acute-phase reactant; not material to this consumer-level claim.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate; clinically useful message.

claims.page_title: Heavy Periods and Iron Deficiency: How a GP Can Help
claims.claim_text: Can contraception be used as treatment? Yes, some hormonal options can reduce bleeding. The best choice depends on your health, side effects and pregnancy plans.

supporting_source.title: Clinical Practice Guidelines: Adolescent gynaecology - heavy menstrual bleeding

claims.evidence_summary: Hormonal methods (combined pill, oral progestogens, levonorgestrel IUS) reduce menstrual blood loss and are standard HMB treatments. The article correctly notes 'some' hormonal options and that choice is individualised.
claims.limitations: Not all hormonal methods reduce bleeding equally; the copper IUD increases it (addressed in WHM-18). The article's 'some' wording is appropriate.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate and appropriately hedged.

claims.page_title: Heavy Periods and Iron Deficiency: How a GP Can Help
claims.claim_text: Heavy periods are also a common cause of iron deficiency and anaemia, which can leave you tired and run down.
claims.evidence_summary: As in WHM-16, healthdirect confirms heavy periods can cause iron deficiency and anaemia, with fatigue among the recognised symptoms. Supported.
claims.limitations: None material.
claims.reviewer_notes: Consistent with WHM-16.

claims.page_title: PCOS and Irregular Periods: What a GP Can Check First
claims.claim_text: Polycystic ovary syndrome represents one potential cause among several possibilities... irregular periods do not necessarily indicate PCOS.
claims.evidence_summary: Irregular cycles have many causes (thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia, hypothalamic dysfunction, perimenopause, pregnancy, etc.); PCOS is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring defined criteria. The article's message that irregular periods do not necessarily mean PCOS is accurate and reduces over-diagnosis.
claims.limitations: None material.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate and protective against self-misdiagnosis.

claims.page_title: PCOS and Irregular Periods: What a GP Can Check First
claims.claim_text: ultrasound findings of polycystic ovaries alone cannot confirm diagnosis. A comprehensive clinical picture is essential.

primary_source.title: Recommendations from the 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for PCOS

claims.evidence_summary: The 2023 guideline requires at least two of: hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction/irregular cycles, and polycystic ovarian morphology (ultrasound or AMH), after excluding other causes. Polycystic ovarian morphology alone is not diagnostic (it is common in the general population). Fully supports the claim.
claims.limitations: None material.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate reflection of current diagnostic criteria.

claims.page_title: PCOS and Irregular Periods: What a GP Can Check First
claims.claim_text: Insulin resistance: A state where the body requires increased insulin for blood sugar management, sometimes associated with PCOS.

primary_source.title: Recommendations from the 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for PCOS

claims.evidence_summary: Insulin resistance is a recognised feature of PCOS pathophysiology and contributes to increased metabolic risk. The article's 'sometimes associated with' is appropriately hedged; the definition of insulin resistance is accurate.
claims.limitations: The 2023 guideline notes clinically available insulin-resistance assays have limited clinical relevance; the article does not recommend testing insulin resistance, which is appropriate.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate lay definition; hedged association.

claims.page_title: PCOS and Irregular Periods: What a GP Can Check First
claims.claim_text: Do I need an ultrasound for PCOS? Not necessarily. Diagnosis depends on age, symptomatology, blood test results and established criteria.

primary_source.title: Recommendations from the 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for PCOS

claims.evidence_summary: The 2023 guideline explicitly states that in patients with irregular menstrual cycles and hyperandrogenism, ovarian ultrasound (and AMH) is not necessary for PCOS diagnosis. Ultrasound is also not recommended for diagnosis within 8 years of menarche. Fully supports the claim.
claims.limitations: Ultrasound remains relevant when only one of the two other criteria is present. The article's 'not necessarily' captures this correctly.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate and reflects the significant 2023 shift reducing unnecessary imaging.

claims.page_title: PCOS and Irregular Periods: What a GP Can Check First
claims.claim_text: The condition extends beyond reproductive organs, potentially affecting menstrual cycles, skin health, hair growth, fertility, insulin sensitivity, cholesterol levels, emotional wellbeing and long-term metabolic functioning.

supporting_source.title: Recommendations from the 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for PCOS

claims.evidence_summary: PCOS is recognised as a multisystem condition affecting menstrual/reproductive function, skin and hair (hyperandrogenism), metabolic health (insulin sensitivity, lipids) and psychological wellbeing (the 2023 guideline highlights higher rates of anxiety and depression). The verb 'potentially affecting' is appropriately hedged.
claims.limitations: Severity and which domains are affected vary widely between individuals.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate multisystem framing.

claims.page_title: Endometriosis Symptoms: Starting the Conversation With Your GP
claims.claim_text: Endometriosis can cause pelvic pain, painful periods, pain with sex, bowel or bladder symptoms, fatigue and fertility concerns.
claims.evidence_summary: Australian sources list severe period pain, chronic pelvic pain, dyspareunia, bowel/bladder symptoms (often cyclical), fatigue and infertility (around 1 in 3 affected have fertility difficulty) among endometriosis features. Fully supports the claim.
claims.limitations: Symptom severity does not correlate with disease extent (see WHM-34); the article addresses this.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate symptom list.

claims.page_title: Endometriosis Symptoms: Starting the Conversation With Your GP
claims.claim_text: Can a GP treat symptoms before diagnosis? Yes. Pain management and hormonal options may be discussed while investigation or referral is underway.

primary_source.title: Australian Living Evidence Guideline: Endometriosis (Clinical Practice Guideline)

claims.evidence_summary: Australian guidance supports empirical/presumptive management of suspected endometriosis - analgesia (including NSAIDs) and hormonal therapies (combined pill, progestogens, levonorgestrel IUS) - without waiting for surgical confirmation. Fully supports the claim.
claims.limitations: Empirical hormonal therapy is a management, not a diagnostic, step; the article frames it correctly as treatment 'while investigation or referral is underway'.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate; consistent with early symptom management.

claims.page_title: Breast Lumps, Breast Pain and Screening: When to See a GP
claims.claim_text: Most breast symptoms are not cancer, but they should still be assessed properly.

primary_source.title: Breast cancer - symptoms, diagnosis, treatment, risk

claims.evidence_summary: healthdirect states 'most breast lumps are not cancerous' while advising review. The article pairs the reassurance with a clear instruction to have symptoms assessed, which matches authoritative advice.
claims.limitations: Reassurance is appropriate but is deliberately balanced with 'should still be assessed properly', avoiding a false-reassurance risk. No harm identified.
claims.reviewer_notes: Well-balanced reassurance-plus-action wording. Low AHPRA risk. Retain the 'but should still be assessed' clause on any future edit so it never reads as bare reassurance.

claims.page_title: Breast Lumps, Breast Pain and Screening: When to See a GP
claims.claim_text: BreastScreen is for screening people without symptoms. A new lump or change should be assessed by a GP so diagnostic imaging can be arranged if needed.
claims.evidence_summary: Consistent with WHS-02; reinforces that symptomatic presentations need diagnostic assessment, not screening. Accurate.
claims.limitations: None material.
claims.reviewer_notes: No change needed.

claims.page_title: Breast Lumps, Breast Pain and Screening: When to See a GP
claims.claim_text: Breast pain is common and often not cancer, but persistent, one-sided or worrying pain should be assessed.

primary_source.title: Breast cancer - symptoms, diagnosis, treatment, risk

claims.evidence_summary: Mastalgia is a common, usually benign presentation; breast pain alone is an uncommon presenting feature of breast cancer. The claim is accurate and appropriately paired with a 'should be assessed' safety net.
claims.limitations: Uses 'common' without quantification, but the statement is epidemiologically accurate and balanced with an assessment prompt, so no false reassurance.
claims.reviewer_notes: Acceptable. Keep the assessment clause.

claims.page_title: Cervical Screening and Self-Collection: A GP Guide for Patients
claims.claim_text: Cervical screening is one of the most important preventive health checks for women and people with a cervix.
claims.recommended_wording: Cervical screening is one of the most effective ways to help prevent cervical cancer for women and people with a cervix.
claims.evidence_summary: Cancer Council notes cervical cancer rates have roughly halved since the program began and the renewed program is expected to reduce deaths further, so a strong benefit statement is defensible. The current wording is an unquantified superlative ('most important preventive health check') presented as benefit without limits.
claims.limitations: Benefit stated without noting screening limitations (screening reduces but does not eliminate risk; symptoms still need separate assessment). The recommended wording ties the benefit to its mechanism (preventing cervical cancer) and softens the superlative while keeping the warm, first-person-adjacent voice.
claims.reviewer_notes: Low-urgency softening. AHPRA advertising guidance cautions against unqualified superlatives; framing the benefit around cancer prevention is safer. The article already states elsewhere that symptoms need separate review, which mitigates the limits concern. [Implemented 2026-09-20; applied to site - see corresponding IND entry.]

claims.page_title: Contraception Options in Australia: How a GP Can Help You Choose
claims.claim_text: Emergency contraception: Contraception used after unprotected sex or contraceptive failure to reduce pregnancy risk.
claims.evidence_summary: Accurate definition of emergency contraception (oral EC or copper IUD used after unprotected sex or method failure to reduce pregnancy risk). 'Reduce pregnancy risk' correctly avoids implying it is fully effective.
claims.limitations: None; 'reduce' is the correct verb (EC is not 100% effective).
claims.reviewer_notes: No change needed.

claims.page_title: Contraception Options in Australia: How a GP Can Help You Choose
claims.claim_text: Can contraception help heavy or painful periods? Some methods can reduce bleeding or pain, but the right choice depends on the cause of symptoms and your medical history.
claims.evidence_summary: Hormonal methods (combined pill, hormonal IUD) can reduce heavy menstrual bleeding and dysmenorrhoea for many people. 'Some methods can reduce ... depends on the cause' is accurate and appropriately conditional.
claims.limitations: None; correctly conditional ('can', 'depends on the cause').
claims.reviewer_notes: No change needed.

claims.page_title: Contraception Options in Australia: How a GP Can Help You Choose
claims.claim_text: Dr Amanda Henderson is trained in Implanon insertion and removal and Mirena removal.
claims.evidence_summary: This is a claim about the practitioner's own training and scope of practice, not a clinical fact verifiable against external literature. It must be substantiated by internal records (training certificates, CPD/procedural logs). It cannot be verified from public authoritative sources and should not be.
claims.limitations: Not verifiable externally by design. The stated scope is internally consistent with the companion article, which says IUD insertion is referred rather than performed - so no scope overstatement is apparent.
claims.reviewer_notes: AHPRA advertising flag: under the National Law (s.133) and AHPRA advertising guidelines, claims about qualifications, training and services must be accurate, verifiable and not misleading. Confirm Dr Henderson holds current, documented competency in Implanon (Nexplanon) insertion/removal and Mirena removal, and that records are on file. Ensure the site does not imply IUD insertion is offered on-site if it is referral-only (the current wording correctly does not). No legal conclusion drawn.

claims.page_title: Contraception Options in Australia: How a GP Can Help You Choose
claims.claim_text: Can I use contraception while breastfeeding? Yes, but not every method is suitable at every stage.
claims.evidence_summary: Consistent with medical eligibility guidance: several methods (e.g. progestogen-only pill, implant, IUD, condoms) are suitable during breastfeeding, while combined hormonal methods are generally avoided in the early postpartum period. 'Not every method is suitable at every stage' is accurate and appropriately conditional.
claims.limitations: None; directs the specifics to an individual GP assessment.
claims.reviewer_notes: No change needed.

claims.page_title: Implanon and IUD Questions: What to Ask Your GP Before Choosing
claims.claim_text: Copper IUDs are non-hormonal but can make periods heavier or more painful for some.
claims.evidence_summary: Heavier and/or more painful periods are a recognised side effect of the copper IUD for some users. Accurate and hedged with 'for some'.
claims.limitations: None.
claims.reviewer_notes: No change needed.

claims.page_title: Implanon and IUD Questions: What to Ask Your GP Before Choosing
claims.claim_text: Is irregular bleeding normal with Implanon? Bleeding changes are common. They may settle, but persistent or troublesome bleeding should be reviewed.
claims.evidence_summary: Unpredictable/irregular bleeding is the most common side effect of the etonogestrel implant and a leading reason for discontinuation; it may improve over time. Accurate, with an appropriate 'should be reviewed' safety net.
claims.limitations: 'Common' is unquantified but epidemiologically accurate for the implant.
claims.reviewer_notes: No change needed.

claims.page_title: Implanon and IUD Questions: What to Ask Your GP Before Choosing
claims.claim_text: Dr Amanda Henderson is trained in Implanon insertion and removal and Mirena removal. If you need an IUD insertion she can discuss referral options.
claims.evidence_summary: Practitioner scope-of-practice statement; substantiate against internal training/competency records. Not externally verifiable and should not be. The paired 'IUD insertion ... discuss referral options' correctly signals that IUD insertion is not performed on-site, so scope is not overstated.
claims.limitations: Not externally verifiable by design.
claims.reviewer_notes: AHPRA advertising flag (as WHS-18): ensure the training claim is documented and current, and that the removal-only vs insertion scope for IUDs is not misread by patients. The current referral caveat is good practice. No legal conclusion drawn.

claims.page_title: Sexual Health, Vaginal Symptoms and STI Testing: A GP Visit Should Feel Safe
claims.claim_text: Symptoms may be due to thrush, bacterial vaginosis, STIs, dermatitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, hormonal changes, contraception, menopause or other causes. Guessing can lead to the wrong treatment.
claims.evidence_summary: The listed differential for vaginal symptoms is clinically accurate and the message that self-diagnosis/pharmacy self-treatment can be wrong (especially for recurrent symptoms) is sound and safety-promoting.
claims.limitations: None; the article avoids diagnostic certainty and encourages assessment.
claims.reviewer_notes: No change needed.

claims.page_title: Sexual Health, Vaginal Symptoms and STI Testing: A GP Visit Should Feel Safe
claims.claim_text: Self-collected swab: A swab taken by the patient after instructions, suitable for some tests. ... Testing may include self-collected swabs, urine tests, blood tests or examination depending on symptoms and risk.
claims.evidence_summary: Self-collected vaginal swabs and first-void urine are validated sample types for certain STI tests (e.g. chlamydia/gonorrhoea NAAT); the appropriate test depends on symptoms and risk. 'Suitable for some tests' is accurate and does not overstate applicability.
claims.limitations: None; correctly limited with 'for some tests'.
claims.reviewer_notes: No change needed.

claims.page_title: Sexual Health, Vaginal Symptoms and STI Testing: A GP Visit Should Feel Safe
claims.claim_text: Can recurrent thrush be something else? Yes. Recurrent symptoms may be thrush, bacterial vaginosis, dermatitis, hormonal changes or another condition, so review is worthwhile.
claims.evidence_summary: Recurrent 'thrush' is frequently misdiagnosed and may represent BV, dermatitis, hormonal/atrophic changes or other conditions; review before repeated self-treatment is appropriate advice. Accurate and safety-promoting.
claims.limitations: None.
claims.reviewer_notes: No change needed.

claims.page_title: ADHD Concerns in Children: First Steps With a GP
claims.claim_text: ADHD: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, involving patterns of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that affect functioning.

primary_source.title: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

claims.evidence_summary: Matches the DSM-5 based definition used by the Australian ADHD Guideline: a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that interferes with functioning or development.
claims.limitations: Simplified plain-language definition.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate. No change needed.

claims.page_title: Childhood Immunisations and Development Checks With a GP
claims.claim_text: Blue book: The NSW personal health record for a child.

primary_source.title: My Personal Health Record (the blue book)

claims.evidence_summary: NSW Health issues the 'My Personal Health Record', widely known as the blue book, to record a child's growth, development and immunisations. Accurate; correctly localised to NSW (South Maroubra practice).
claims.limitations: Terminology is state-specific; correct for NSW patients.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate. No change needed.

claims.page_title: Childhood Immunisations and Development Checks With a GP
claims.claim_text: Dr Amanda Henderson undertakes development checks with scheduled immunisations and takes parental concerns seriously.

primary_source.title: Practice service description - not an external clinical claim

claims.evidence_summary: This is a statement of services offered by the practice, not a clinical/scientific claim, so it cannot be verified against an external authority. It should be confirmed as accurate by Dr Henderson/practice. Undertaking developmental surveillance at immunisation visits is consistent with RACGP Red Book preventive-care practice.
claims.limitations: Accuracy is a matter of practice fact; verify internally.
claims.reviewer_notes: Confirm with the practice that this reflects actual service provision (AHPRA advertising must be truthful). No safety issue with the wording itself.

claims.page_title: Starting Solids and Allergy Foods: Calm Advice for Parents
claims.claim_text: Readiness signs: Signs a baby may be ready for solids, such as sitting with support and showing interest in food. Responsive feeding: Following a baby's cues for interest, hunger and fullness.

primary_source.title: How to Introduce Solid Foods to Babies

supporting_source.title: Introducing solids: why, when, what and how

claims.evidence_summary: Readiness signs (able to sit with support and hold head steady, showing interest in food, reaching/opening mouth) and responsive feeding (following the baby's hunger/fullness cues) are standard descriptions consistent with ASCIA and Raising Children Network. Accurate.
claims.limitations: Plain-language definitions.
claims.reviewer_notes: Accurate. No change needed.

claims.page_title: Baby and Childhood Eczema: Getting the Basics Right
claims.claim_text: Emollient: A moisturiser used to repair and protect the skin barrier. Wet dressing: A technique sometimes used for more severe eczema under medical guidance.
claims.evidence_summary: Accurate: emollients repair/protect the skin barrier and are first-line; wet dressings (wet wraps) are used for more severe or resistant eczema and should be done with clinical guidance. Consistent with RCH.
